```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The 90-day goal favors a single-sided product. B needs one reader to pay about $5/month. A needs a buyer and a seller to both show up and a deal to close before the seller-pays-at-close fee earns anything. Brief A names buyer-side liquidity as the documented failure mode.",
    "A's own evidence argues against it. The closest comparable, DealMyApp, reports 500+ visitors a day and about 30 listings, but buyers are 'slower to convert.' A $750 paid test to a similar audience produced 124 clicks and zero sales. B has no equivalent documented conversion failure.",
    "A cannot earn early revenue through upfront fees. Three of the five live competitors charge 0% or near-0% commission or are free to list, so a listing fee faces free alternatives. B has a sourced direct price anchor, Edition.ink's $5/month Pro tier, at a low enough price for a first test sale.",
    "B's acquisition channels have sourced, cheap, granular costs. Nextdoor is $2-5 CPC and Facebook about $0.70-1.14 CPC, so a single zip code can be tested within budget. A's only costed channel is the $750 newsletter placement that produced zero sales, and its Product Hunt entry has no outcome data.",
    "B's buildability is better evidenced. Multiple solo-developer open-source clones show the ingest-to-edition pipeline can be built quickly with AI tools. A's evidence for buildability rests on one solo-built comparable that is struggling to convert buyers.",
    "B carries real risks that keep this from being a strong win. Copyright exposure from AI-rewriting scraped news, free open-source substitutes, and old demand evidence about print papers rather than personalized digital editions all weaken it. These threaten scale more than they threaten landing a first paying customer."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea A's central differentiation claim has no supporting data. The brief asserts that AI agents can replicate Acquire.com's human 'acquisition expert' services (listing optimization, buyer vetting, deal coaching) at near-zero marginal cost. It cites only Acquire.com's pricing page, which shows those services exist but not that they can be automated or that buyers would trust an automated version. Every other differentiation lever, price and niche, is undercut by the brief's own competitor table.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate to low confidence. Both briefs show crowded markets and weak differentiation. B's demand quotes are 2008-2017 complaints about print papers, not evidence of willingness to pay for this product. B's Pew '~9% pay for local news' figure has no URL, so I treated it as unsourced. The litigation references also lack links. Neither brief gives a conversion rate for its own model. B wins mainly because a single-sided $5 subscription is a shorter path to a first payment than a two-sided marketplace that earns at close. A's evidence specifically documents the conversion failure that would block that path."
}
```
